items.title: Bulk migrate branch protections to rulesets for a repository
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now convert all branch protection rules of a repository to rulesets in a single action. This is an extension of the ability to convert a single branch protection rule to a ruleset that we released previously, now allowing for at-scale conversions. How it works Navigate to Settings → Rulesets in your repository and click Import branch protection rules. In the Review import dialog, you can: Preview the rulesets that will be created before you confirm the conversion. See which branch protection rules are already covered by an existing ruleset. Review cases where one branch protection rule produces multiple rulesets to preserve its original behavior. Choose an enforcement status (e.g., Active, Evaluate, or Disabled) and select which rulesets to create. After you click Create rulesets, choose whether to keep or delete the original branch protection rules. Why migrate to rulesets? Rulesets offer several advantages over classic branch protections: Apply rules across multiple branches with pattern matching Layer multiple rulesets for granular policy control Manage rulesets at the organization or enterprise level Configure fine-grained bypass permissions for users, teams, and apps Availability This feature is available for all repositories where rulesets are available. Learn more about converting your branch protections to repository rulesets. Join the discussion within GitHub Community. The post Bulk migrate branch protections to rulesets for a repository appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Dependabot alerts REST API now includes dependency versions
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now get the version of a vulnerable dependency directly from Dependabot alert responses in the REST API. Each alert’s dependency object includes a new version_requirement field with the version or version constraint that Dependabot last recorded for the alert. Alert responses already included the advisory’s vulnerable version range, but not the version in your repository. If you sync alerts to other security tools, you no longer need to parse lockfiles or make a separate GraphQL request for vulnerableRequirements to get that version. The value depends on how Dependabot detected the dependency: Lockfiles: The resolved version. Manifests without a lockfile: The version or version constraint declared in the manifest. Dependency submission API: The resolved version submitted by your build tooling. The field is null when no value is available. If an alert covers more than one vulnerable version of a dependency, the field holds one recorded value and may not represent all of them. Long version constraints may also be truncated. You’ll find version_requirement in responses for individual alerts, in repository, organization, and enterprise alert lists, and in dependabot_alert webhook payloads. This field is available now on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24. Learn more about the REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts and the dependabot_alert webhook event. The post Dependabot alerts REST API now includes dependency versions appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: GitHub package firewall in public preview
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: An increasing number of malware attacks exploit systems at package installation time, harvesting credentials on CI/CD hosts or developer workstations without even running the package’s code. To stem this tide of attacks, GitHub is introducing a new package firewall capability. The package firewall sits between endpoints like Actions runners or coding agents and the upstream package repositories, inspecting both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity. The package firewall is available today in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud. How it works First, administrators set policy controls for their enterprise. The controls available today include a configurable cooldown period, checking the GitHub Advisory Database for malware or vulnerability alerts, and supply-chain checks like attestation downgrades. Then endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts need configuration to use the firewall for their requests instead of pointing directly at the upstream package registries. Metadata requests for package lists as well as the actual package downloads then flow through the firewall, which evaluates them against the policy. If a package is blocked erroneously, the user can request an exception with a workflow similar to other GitHub Advanced Security features. Availability and limitations The package firewall is available in public preview as we scale up the infrastructure behind it and continue to add features based on customer demand. It is available to GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. The service is free while in the preview period. When it reaches general availability, it will be charged based on metered usage, similar to Actions billing. Currently the package firewall only supports npm packages. How to use it For detailed setup instructions, see Protecting endpoints with package firewall. Join the discussion in Git

items.title: Updates to GitHub secret scanning
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: This update covers improvements and bug fixes for GitHub secret scanning. Update to audit log events On November 12, 2026, the business field in affected secret_scanning_alert.* and secret_scanning_push_protection.bypass audit log events will change from the enterprise display name to the enterprise slug. To avoid disruption to any automated workflows, you should update integrations that filter by display name before rollout to accept both formats or use business_id instead. The business field remains a string. Event names and numeric business_id values are unchanged. Recent improvements and bug fixes Custom pattern alerts: Existing open alerts stay open when a rescan finds that they still match an edited custom pattern, rather than being closed and reopened. Base64-encoded GitHub tokens: In private and internal repositories on github.com with secret scanning enabled, the existing revocation action (public preview) now supports encoded personal access tokens (classic), fine-grained personal access tokens, OAuth access tokens, and GitHub App user access tokens. GitHub automatically decodes the value. Dismissal-request webhooks: Payloads now include exemption_request.number, the repository-scoped request number also available in the REST API. Use the repository and request number together to correlate requests across integrations. Accessibility: The Request pending status on an alert is now keyboard-focusable without activating an action. The revocation flow announces progress to screen readers and moves focus to its completion panel when that panel appears. Bypass-request metadata: Fixed empty secret-type and location details in bypass-request API responses and webhook payloads for command-line pushes when another repository rule ran after secret scanning. request failing on Vertex, Bedrock and other providers when the endpoint or a gateway rejects tool search, and behind gateways with ToolSearch disallowed or left out of --tools (a 2.1.304 regression): Claude Code now retries without it Fixed /effort and /autocompact settings not applying when the model name differed from a modelOverrides value by letter case or a [1m] tag Fixed new worktrees in a bare repository sometimes starting from local HEAD instead of the default branch, and unchanged subagent worktrees sometimes not being cleaned up Fixed Bash commands on a full disk failing with a raw ENOSPC file path: the error now says the disk is full and that nothing ran Fixed an MCP server passed by a cloud session or by the SDK's setMcpServers being replaced later in the session by a same-named server from your own settings Fixed Claude naming the wrong model for a subagent's work after the subagent switched to a fallback model Fixed cloud sessions and teammates not telling Claude when a compaction had to leave the oldest messages out of its summary to fit Fixed more cases of scheduled Cowork cloud sessions waiting five minutes for each subagent whose WebFetch needed a URL items.title: My obituary for programming
items.excerpt: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming, careers, ai, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, deep-blue
items.why_it_matters: Reflective opinion piece on how coding agents change the craft of programming. Relevant to our AI-native culture and career conversations, but no actionable technical content.

items.title: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute
items.excerpt: This was recorded on the sidelines of the new Compute Trading track at AIE NYC. Catch us next at AIE CODE, our last flagship for the top agentic engineers in the world.In the early days of cloud, former guest Martin Casado made something so disruptive that Cisco was threatened enough to pay $600m for it, and VMware outbid for $1.3B:That concept was software-defined networking, which virtualized the routing network by separating the control plane from the data plane. That revolution is now coming for GPUs - where previously running your own supercompute cluster required $50-100m upfront to get commitments and do the entire stack from hardware to firmware to kernels, SF Compute is now enabling you to not only buy or sell GPU hours now and in the future, but also to programmatically control everything from your network to memory.We last spoke with Evan about commoditizing compute. At AI Engineer New York, we went deeper: what does it take to physically deliver a GPU contract, and what has to be true before a market in compute can become liquid?From selling a room to running the hotelEvan describes SF Compute’s expansion with a hotel analogy. A customer wants a room, then asks for cleaning, room service, and security. Eventually you discover that delivering the room means operating the hotel. SF Compute began by trying to sublease a cluster; the company has since built much of the operating capacity of a cloud to deliver the compute traded on its market.That work is physical settlement: the buyer gets usable compute, rather than simply a cash payment against an index. It brings the physical constraints of a cluster into the market itself. Can a workload be interrupted? How quickly can it recover from storage? Which GPU generation, networking and software configuration does it need? items.title: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute

items.excerpt: GPU compute is bought and sold like a commodity, but delivering it is a lot messier than trading a contract. We cover: • Why SF Compute had to build cloud operations to deliver the GPUs it trades • How interruptions, storage and hardware generations affect compute prices • Why batch and live inference need different contract terms • Physical versus cash settlement, and the risk of trading a price disconnected from actual GPUs • Why NVIDIA and the big clouds have different incentives from an independent market • How to turn a data center into a programmable GPU cluster Chapters: 0:00 Why can’t NVIDIA build this? 0:25 Welcome back to Latent Space 2:23 From selling a room to running the hotel 3:47 Physical settlement: actually delivering compute 6:00 Liquidity and the GPU order book 8:42 Trading nonstandard compute 10:00 Interrupting and moving workloads 12:20 Why hardware cohorts matter 14:32 How far out do compute contracts go? 16:19 Batch versus live inference leases 17:58 The shape of compute prices 20:33 GPU generations, specifications and SKUs 23:30 Physical versus cash settlement 27:00 The emerging compute market ecosystem 29:03 What it takes to deliver a GPU cluster 32:24 Sovereign compute 33:26 Why NVIDIA can’t build this market 34:48 A programmable data center SF Compute: https://sfcompute.com Latent Space: https://www.latent.space Sponsorship and business inquiries: business@latent.space
